response.query: Should sampling be at repository or package/module level for monorepos; how to compute N_stratum and post-stratification weights when repos contain variable package counts, and should cluster-robust SEs be used?
response.answer: Sampling should be at the package level in monorepos; compute N_stratum using population counts; use cluster-robust SEs for valid inference.

results.content: # Using post-stratification weights in R survey package. I am analyzing a dataset that has a variable for post-stratification weights. Its weight is a post-stratification weight accounting for probability of selection, unit non-responses, and post-stratifies the sample to match the age and gender joint distribution. So my question is: Am I safe, or roughly safe, using the provided post-stratification weight in the `svydesign(weights=)` argument? As @StasK says, the correct standard errors for raked/calibrated weights depend on the original weights and the auxiliary variables, and you don't get the right standard errors just by treating them as sampling weights. $\begingroup$ It's pretty standard in official statistics and public opinion research to just treat post-stratified weights as sampling weights. > "Public-use data sets often come with weights that have been adjusted by post-stratification, raking, or calibration. results.title: What is the difference between monoliths, microservices, monorepos and multirepos? - DEV Community
results.content: # What is the difference between monoliths, microservices, monorepos and multirepos? ## Is a monorepo a monolith? A monolith can be broken up into microservices, but a monorepo can only be broken down into individual repositories. The opposite of a monorepo is a multirepo (or a polyrepo) and the opposite of a monolith is distributed microservices. Monoliths have tightly coupled code bases which can only be decoupled by distributed microservices not by polyrepos or monorepos. A monorepo is often mistakenly thought to be a monolith - this is when code is colocated with no clear establishment of the relationship or use of such a stratgey. These articles may be useful in determining how and when your use case fits a monorepo, polyrepo or monolith structure. * A demo of how the 3 systems work - monorepos, multirepos and monoliths. Concrete software examples of Monolith, Monorepo, Multirepo and Microservices would help to understand the meta-level concepts described in your article.

results.title: Why you should use survey weights in UX research - Carl J. Pearson, PhD
results.content: # Why you should use survey weights in UX research. Traditional survey weighting approaches were developed in demography and political science domains, so demographics are of key importance in that domain and the only kinds of variables with population level measures available to researchers (necessary for weighting). In UX research, we almost always know our variables of importance from our log data – that makes our weights stratification weights. Note: you can calculate your weights to give the proportion from sample invites to sampling stratum, but calculating it so each response maps to a real count of users in the population is the desired format. Non-response weights account for when fewer users in a sample, or stratified sub-sample, respond to a survey compared to the invited number. There are more population weight calculation methods that could be relevant in UX research than design or non-response weights. Calibration is a method that uses inverse probabilities to make the sums of users in weighting variables match the population totals for users in those variables. The main conceptual difference is that you create your stratification weights as you create the sample (like we talked about regarding design weights), so you create the weights before you even send the survey. Stratification design weights are often calculated in the same way as post-stratification population weights when your sampling frame is identical to your population. Technically, when you have the data available, you can or should do a 3 step process of calculating design weights, non-response weights, and then population weights. Using the post-stratification procedure in the R package survey, you can account for the design/population weights (when population = sampling frame) and the survey non-response rates in a single step. 5. In R, bring in the survey response data that contains key weighting variables attached for each respondent. 7. Use the `survey` package to calculate weights (technically using the post-stratification method for population weights, but realistically covering design and non-response weights in 1 step). Ultimately, your variable selection is more important than weight calculation procedures and we don’t need to use ML to make effective survey weights most of the time.
